title: Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty
one_liner: A $1 refractometer reading at day 3-5 predicts whether a $1,400 crossbred calf lives, yet nobody independently verifies it at sale. Own that measurement and the warranty that follows.
customer: Calf raisers, backgrounders and feeder buyers who pay a premium for graded calves (or a subscription for the data), and dairies who pay to have calves graded so they can earn the premium. Later, insurers and MGAs underwriting a mortality warranty.
problem: Beef-on-dairy calf output went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to roughly 3.2M in 2024, with CattleFax projecting 5-6M, and calves have sold as high as $1,500 per head. Calf raisers buy 3-5 day old calves nearly blind and eat the 10-25% loss to scours and pneumonia. The colostrum information stays on the dairy, so raisers blame 'bad calves' and dairies blame 'bad luck'. Each dead calf now leaves a four-figure hole in a heifer pipeline that is short by hundreds of thousands of head.
solution: Independent serum total protein (Brix) testing on every calf at day 3-5, done at the dairy or at pickup by trained techs with digital refractometers and a phone app. Each calf is graded on the published four-tier passive-transfer scale (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor) and logged with dairy, sire, weight and hydration score, then gets a QR tag or passport that follows the calf to the buyer. Buyers pay a premium for Excellent and Good and discount Poor. Phase 2 uses the accumulated data to price a 30- or 60-day mortality warranty ('we have graded 300,000 calves and know what a Brix 8.4 calf from Dairy X does'). Phase 3 gives dairies a colostrum scorecard that brokers use.
why_now: Crossbred calves are at record values, beef-on-dairy volume is doubling, and the heifer shortage means every lost calf is expensive and hard to replace. Consensus passive-transfer grading standards were published in 2020, digital refractometers are cheap, and buyers are already paying for verified genetics programs, so 'verified immunity' is the obvious next tag that nobody sells.
revenue_model: $4-6 per calf grading fee paid by the seller or split with the buyer, then $10-25 per calf warranty premium once loss data supports underwriting (partner with an insurer or MGA rather than carrying risk), plus a data subscription for larger calf raisers and feedlots.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone argues about sire genetics while the vet knows immune status dominates early death, and calves with failure of passive transfer carry about twice the risk of illness and death. The test is $1 and 60 seconds, but a number only has value when a neutral third party holds custody of it at the point of sale. The business is independent custody of the measurement, not the refractometer, and the resulting dataset becomes the underwriting moat.
first_30_days: Two vet techs, two $150 digital refractometers and a phone form. Offer free grading on 5 dairies' weekly calf shipments to 2-3 calf raisers or brokers. Ask the raiser to report 30-day illness and death by calf tag. After about 60 days, publish graded-versus-ungraded outcomes, then get one raiser to commit to a premium (for example $30-50) for Excellent calves and a discount for Poor, and charge the test fee from that point on.

tournament.cluster: Farm and ranch risks: disease, cash, storage and machinery
judge_notes: vc: rank 2/25 - Sharp, non-consensus, real four-figure loss per calf; custody of the measurement builds an underwriting data moat.
operator: rank 3/25 - Tiny cheap test, huge calf volume, real four-figure losses, scrappy pilot with two vet techs and instant proof.
contrarian: rank 1/25 - Dismissible $1 refractometer, yet a real beef-on-dairy boom; neutral custody of the number becomes a data and warranty moat.

competitors.name: Where Food Comes From (third-party verification: Age Verification, Source Verification, USDA Process Verified Program, custom Process Verified claims)
competitors.what_they_do: Established independent verifier of cattle and food claims. Its program list has age, source, natural, feed and welfare verification. It has no calf passive-transfer or immunity-grading program. Its custom 'Process Verified' program could be used to audit a graded-calf claim, so it is the nearest incumbent that could bolt this on.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established, multi-program company. Revenue and funding were not verified in this session.

competitors.name: Calftech Corporation (Central Valley, CA calf ranch)
competitors.what_they_do: A vertically integrated calf-ranch operator that competes on the health of its calf-ranch graduates. The article credits it with the lowest liver-abscess rates 'by a wide margin'. It sells outcomes from its own rearing system, not independent day-3-to-5 immunity grading. It shows that big raisers can keep their own health data in-house instead of buying it from a neutral third party.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Private operator. Scale was not verified, and its website returned 503.

competition.white_space:
Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement.
competition.evidence_of_demand:
Supportive evidence found:
- Packers already penalise unknown health history. Progressive Dairy reports 'standardized fee deduction[s]' on beef-on-dairy cattle with unknown health histories or generic genetics, and says premium pricing requires documented, traceable, value-added product (https://agproud.com/articles/54216-beef-on-dairy-calves-cause-supply-chain-problems). This is the strongest sign that buyers discount for missing records.
- Health records are cited as a possible premium lever. Dairies 'know everything that happens to those calves', and records could earn a premium, though the article gives no dollar figure (https://agproud.com/articles/55435-pushing-for-a-better-premium-beef-on-dairy and https://agproud.com/articles/30838-beef-on-dairy-done-right-how-to-make-the-crossbred-calf-the-market-desires).
- Real dispersion in immunity means grading would carry information. In a 2025 Indiana and Michigan study of 355 calves, 20.8% were Excellent, 25.4% Good, 26.5% Fair and 27.3% Poor by serum total protein. Dairy-beef crossbreds and purebred dairy calves did not differ. Feeding colostrum within 1 hour after birth cut the odds of a lower category (OR 0.48) (Kern et al., Transl Anim Sci 2025, PMID 40575029).
- The four-tier standard is confirmed. Lombard et al. 2020 (J Dairy Sci, PMID 32448583) define Excellent at 25 g/L IgG or more, Good at 18.0 to 24.9, Fair at 10.0 to 17.9 and Poor below 10. Herd goals are more than 40%, 30%, 20% and under 10% of calves. The paper gives on-farm serum total protein and %Brix equivalents.

Weak or missing evidence:
- No evidence found of buyers paying a dollar premium for Brix-graded calves, or of an RFP, a forum complaint thread or a spend line for independent grading.
- The idea's figures (3.2M head in 2024, $1,500 calves, 10-25% raiser loss) were not verified. One Progressive Dairy snippet puts US pre-weaning calf mortality at 6-8% against a 3% target (https://agproud.com/articles/36208-calf-mortality-can-it-be-too-low). That figure is for dairy calves generally, so the 10-25% raiser-loss claim needs a source.
- Feeders are told not to assume crossbreds earn a premium over the Holstein base price (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). That is a headwind for a graded-calf premium.
- Several of the more relevant articles are paywalled, so I could not read their loss and cost figures.
competition.sharper_angle:
Lead with the data and dispute layer and defer the warranty. Sell to the dairy, not the raiser. Dairies are the party facing packer and buyer discounts for unknown health history, and they have the incentive to prove colostrum quality.
1. Product: an independent day-3-to-5 STP/Brix grade on the Lombard four-tier scale, logged per calf with dairy, sire and colostrum-timing fields. It is sold as a dairy 'colostrum scorecard' that earns contract terms with calf ranches and feeders. The buyer-facing calf passport comes second.
2. Wedge market: sale-barn and broker lots where the buyer has no bilateral history with the dairy. In contracted dairy-to-ranch flows, source reputation already does the job.
3. Position as a neutral referee, not a data vendor. Build lot-level dispute settlement at arrival, with a chain-of-custody sample and a fixed rejection or discount schedule. That is the one thing a raiser cannot do alone for $1.
4. Warranty later, via an MGA, and only on graded calves. Cover a narrow perils window, such as scours and pneumonia deaths within 30 days. Exclude raiser-management causes, or require the raiser to share the risk.
5. Distribution: partner with a verifier such as Where Food Comes From, or with a calf-ranch network, so it is not competing head-on with the nearest incumbent.
Before building, get one buyer to state a dollar-per-head premium for Excellent calves and a discount for Poor. The 60-day outcome study in the 30-day plan should be treated as a go/no-go gate. Also verify the market-size and loss-rate figures and run the search-based checks I could not: Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, calf-ranch vendors and private livestock mortality insurers.
